extracted.intended_audience: princes, statesmen, and learned scholars (rulers and divines)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance for rulers, lawmakers, and theologians on pursuing fortune, governing, drafting laws, and interpreting Scripture; a mix of political prudence, legal craft, and limits on reason in divinity. The page gives prescriptive rules and criticisms aimed at improving practical statecraft and theological method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid single-minded pursuit; remain opportunistic
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not mind actions wholly one by one; avoid losing intervening occasions by being fixated on a single action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “For he that doth so loseth infinite occasions which intervene, and are many times more proper and propitious...” — keep a broad view and be ready to seize better opportunities that intervene rather than rigidly following one immediate plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always preserve an exit or retreat
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not engage peremptorily; ever have a window to fly out at or a way to retire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit precept: maintain options and contingency plans (illustrated by the fable of the two frogs); never bind oneself so absolutely that there is no retreat if circumstances change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate cautious, moderate attachments (operative 'bias')
rubrics_metrics.description: Love as if the beloved might be a future enemy, and hate as if one might become a lover—i.e., practise caution and moderation in friendships and rivalries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Et ama tanquam inimicus futurus et odi tanquam amaturus.’ Avoid excessive embroilment in unfortunate friendships, spleens, childish envies, or emulations that betray utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer fair and durable means over corrupt shortcuts
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject evil or perfidious arts even if they may attain fortune more quickly; the shortest way is commonly the fouler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of Machiavellian maxims (appearance vs reality of virtue, sowing thorns, deceits) — while evil arts may make fortune more hasty and compendious, they are morally and practically inferior and often self-defeating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temper pursuit of fortune with religious and philosophical priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Place divine and moral goods before the pursuit of fortune; 'Primum quærite regnum Dei' and 'Primum quærite bona animi.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not sacrifice devotional duties or moral foundations to gain wealth or power; the divine foundation is the firm rock compared to the sands of human foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulers should make public matters as manifest as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: In governors towards the governed, things ought as far as possible to be manifest and revealed (people’s natures, conditions, factions, animosities, discontents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency toward wise senates and councils is recommended because knowledge of the people's dispositions aids governance; reserve applies more to certain secret or hard-to-know aspects of government, but public-facing clarity is a virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge secrecy: some matters of government are rightly reserved
rubrics_metrics.description: Some aspects of governance are obscure or unfit to utter and require reverent/reserved handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes secrets that are hard to know from secrets unfit to be uttered; private prudence is necessary in certain statecraft matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law-making must be practical and consider execution
rubrics_metrics.description: The wisdom of a law-maker includes not only principles of justice but their application: how laws may be made certain, apt, and easy to be executed; causes and remedies of doubtfulness and impediments in execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawmakers should think about clearness, certainty, executability, and remedies for ambiguity; treat legal drafting as practical engineering, not merely philosophical speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design laws with appropriate form and concision
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether laws should be penned in texts or Acts, brief or large, with preambles or without; keep them from being too vast or full of multiplicity and crossness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law format decisions matter for comprehension and administration; prune and reform laws from time to time to avoid over-bloating legal codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide rules for legal exposition and mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide how laws are to be expounded (judicially vs by conferences), whether to press rigorously or tenderly, and the role of equity versus strict law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine when discretion should be used and whether discretion and strict law are mingled in the same courts or kept separate; consider equity and good conscience as mitigation where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Govern the legal profession and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice, profession, and erudition of law should be censured and governed as part of law-making wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider standards of training, practice, and oversight to ensure the legal system functions; law isn't only texts—it's animated by practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of reducing complex knowledge (divinity) into an artificial method
rubrics_metrics.description: Reducing divinity to exact methods or sums (an art) tends to obscure, corrupt, or make knowledge more immense but less substantial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summaries and methods promise brevity and strength but often produce greater volumes and weaker grounds; such art-like compaction is acceptable for introductions, but dangerous for the main body of divinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground divinity on the Word of God rather than natural reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Sacred theology is grounded upon the word and oracle of God, not upon the light of nature; faith addresses matters beyond natural reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faith requires assent even where reason resists; the moral law as revealed surpasses the capacity of natural reason to fully determine duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use human reason in spiritual things, but only secondarily
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason in religion has two uses: to illustrate and help conceive mysteries (not to argue their truth), and to make derivative inferences after principles are laid down; it is secondary and respective, not original and absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not subject first principles of divinity to the same inductive/syllogistic scrutiny appropriate to natural philosophy; reason may illuminate but not replace revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define limits and proper use of reason in divinity
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a deficiency in not sufficiently inquiring into the true limits and use of reason in spiritual things; this should be treated as a 'divine dialectic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properly delineating where reason may operate (illustration, inference) prevents both overcurious speculation and the abuse of religious authority to silence legitimate opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish fundamental from non-fundamental doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: Points fundamental to religion should be distinguished from points of further perfection to reduce controversies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat fundamental points with strictness ('He that is not with us is against us'), whereas non-fundamental matters should be handled charitably ('He that is not against us is with us'); this reduces heat in disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'positive divinity'—brief, text-based observations—to scholastic commonplaces
rubrics_metrics.description: The most valuable form in divinity is positive divinity: brief observations collected on particular texts, not dilated into commonplaces or reduced into method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such writing is rich and precious, suited to sermons and works that endure; avoid prolix commentaries and argumentative method that chase controversies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize multiple legitimate senses in Scripture while exercising caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture contains literal, moral, allegorical/typical, and anagogical senses; interpreters must allow moral and sometimes allegorical senses but be cautious of excessive allegory or physical/philosophical readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literal sense is main stream; moral, allegorical, and anagogical senses supply further doctrine distributively; avoid overly curious or unsafe interpretations that stretch beyond sobriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not extract natural philosophy from Scripture
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a mistake to seek the truths of natural philosophy in the Scriptures; the Author’s authority in one domain is not authority in another: 'Auctoris aliud agentis parva auctoritas.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scripture is ordered to moral and divine instruction; using it as a primary source for natural physics or temporal matters leads to error and demeans both Scripture and natural philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for the distributive richness of Scripture (secrets and succession of ages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Scripture was written with foresight of heresies, Church states, and the elect, it carries distributive springs of doctrine in clauses and words beyond immediate context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation should not be limited only to immediate occasion, context, or strict literal sense; be open to meanings that serve future ages and varied circumstances, while avoiding excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of summary brevity that generates obscurity
rubrics_metrics.description: Summaries intended to abridge often become obscure and require expansive commentary, resulting in works larger than originals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that contraction tends to breed dilution and exposition; use summaries primarily as introductions, not as substitutes for engagement with primary texts.
